label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# Cup Day, The Coolroom, and Me Doing Your Job

Jonno, you've been messaging me for a week asking what happened on Cup Day, and I've been putting it off because typing it all out is a nightmare. So here it is, on the blog, where forty people can read it, most of whom are you and Mum. Enjoy.

Monday night, the coolroom compressor died. Just quit. Nobody knows why, and nobody's going to find out, because it's a compressor and they don't tell you anything. Tuesday morning at 6.40am I walked in on Cup Day, which is already the busiest day of the year, and the thermometer said 11 degrees. Eleven. Hot dairy is not a vibe, mate.

We had 140 covers booked for lunch. Set menu, three courses, the whole production. And the fridge guy, Wally from Coldline, could not come until Wednesday because the part was coming from Sydney. Sydney. Who orders a compressor part from Sydney? Apparently the entire industry does, and nobody warned us.

So we did what bistro kitchens always do. We moved everything into the two undercounters, the bar fridge, and then Marta's cafe next door let us use half her walk-in. Which was a lifesaver until you remember you have to carry everything next door in the middle of service prep. I've never moved so much cold stuff so fast in my life, and I was doing it in a Cup Day hat that was not designed for this.

We still lost about eighteen hundred bucks of stock. Mostly dairy and the duck legs. The duck legs, Jonno. Forty-odd kilos of duck legs, and I had to stand there and watch them go in the bin like they'd personally let me down.

Raff was off that day, so guess who was running the pass? Me. Sous-chef, twenty-nine years old, running a 140-cover set menu with a dishwasher who thinks he's a comedian and a bar fridge that sounds like it's about to take off. I'd like to say I handled it with grace. I did not. But I did handle it, and that's the bit I'm weirdly proud of.

The beef situation deserves its own paragraph. Thirty kilos of beef shin needed to get from the cold storage to the prep area, which was down the laneway, and the only thing we had was a milk crate on a trolley. It was raining. Me and Benny carried that trolley down the laneway like two blokes moving a piano, and halfway there one of the wheels fell off. We just kept going. The beef made it. The dignity did not.

Kev filled the old esky with ice from the servo. Fourteen bags. The servo guy looked at us, looked at the esky, and asked if we were having a party. We said yeah, mate, a party for a hundred and forty people, and he just nodded slowly like he'd seen some things.

Then, at 12.15, we had to 86 the panna cotta. Gone. Dessert became "affogato with whatever," and honestly, people loved it more. I don't know what that says about panna cotta, but it's not good news for the panna cotta.

There was a lady on table 9 who asked if the beef was "free range from the laneway" because she'd seen us out the window with the trolley. I didn't have the heart to tell her no. I just said yes. We're basically a farm-to-table restaurant now.

Marta, bless her, made us pay her back for the walk-in space in croissant credit. I now owe her about three weeks of staff meal. I'm going to be eating croissants until I die, and I'm not even mad about it.

And the sweep. My horse was called Ice Cold Lad. I picked it because of the coolroom situation, which I thought was a clever bit of irony, and it came second last. Second last. The universe is taking the piss, and it's taking the piss specifically on the day I'm already having the worst day of my life.

Phil, the owner, kept saying "just make it work, mate." That is not a plan, Jonno. That's a vibe. I love Phil, but "make it work" is what people say when they have no idea what's happening in the kitchen and they want to go home early.

Here's the thing, though. It was honestly the best service we did all year. Everyone was locked in. Nobody panicked out loud, the boys just kept moving, and every plate that went out was tight. Benny was calling orders like he was in a war film. Kev was doing the esky runs without being asked. Even the bar staff were pitching in on prep. You don't get that kind of focus when things are going well. You get it when everything's on fire and you've all decided to fight it together.

Anyway, I'm not saying you'd have loved it, but I know you would've lost your mind. You'd have been on the phone to Phil before the compressor even stopped making noise, and you'd have wanted to fix the trolley with a bread tie, and you'd have cried a little when the duck legs went in the bin. London has made you soft, mate. Don't pretend otherwise. I've seen your Instagram. There's a flat white with a fern on it.

That's the whole story. Sorry it took a blog post, but I'm not typing this out twice, and you're the only one who gets how bad it was.

Come home ya flog.
